newsitem.title: GERMANY: Banker says Euro bank may need inflation goal.
newsitem.headline: Banker says Euro bank may need inflation goal.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher said on Thursday that the future European central bank may need to adopt an inflation as well as money supply target to ensure its credibility in the first years of monetary union.

Transition to monetary union will lead to a change in monetary relations between member states and diminish the indicator function of money supply, he said in the text of a speech prepared for a banking conference.
"For this reason potential-oriented money supply targeting -- at least in the first years after the launch of EMU -- would be confronted with considerable problems," he added.

Kuehbacher, who is head of the state central bank of Berlin and Brandenburg, said divergences from the money supply target had not led to a loss of credibility in the case of the Bundesbank, but could damage a new central bank that had not had time to build up such a reputation.
It might make sense therefore to complement an interim target like money supply with an inflation target to counter initial uncertainty over monetary relations, he said.

Kuehbacher suggested offering three-month tenders for securities repurchase agreements, or repos, alongside shorter repo tenders. Longer tenders would make it easier for smaller banks not active in the money market to gain access to central bank funds.
The banker said private sector securities should be allowed in addition to public debt as eligible collateral for central bank loans.

The Bundesbank regarded the introduction of a minimum reserve requirement for the European monetary union area as indispensable because it would create a sufficient and predictable demand for central bank funds, he said.
The requirement would ensure steady demand for central bank money at a time when the use of electronic money and prepaid cards was on the increase and causing a decline in cash circulation, he added.
Kuehbacher said the banking system's dependence on central banks for refinancing was declining.
"But it is exactly this dependence which secures the central bank's influence on money market interest rates, and through this on other interest rates."

Countering criticism that the minimum reserve increases banks' costs and distorts competition with other banking centres, Kuehbacher said the problem could be reduced if minimum reserve rates were kept low and applied broadly across the European Union.
Kuehbacher said the Council of the European Monetary Institute had decided to give the European central bank the option of levying the minimum reserve.
